title: Wildfire Fallout and a Reality TV Challenger Shake Up LA Mayor's Race
summary: The race for mayor of Los Angeles has taken a surreal turn. Incumbent Karen Bass, the first Black woman to lead the city, is battling to keep her job against a field of 14 challengers—including Spencer Pratt, the reality TV star best known for "The Hills." Pratt's Pacific Palisades home was among the thousands destroyed in last year's catastrophic wildfire, and he has made Bass's leadership during the crisis a central issue. Bass was in Ghana as part of a presidential delegation when the fire erupted, a trip that has fueled perceptions of detachment. Pratt, a registered Republican, has leaned into his celebrity, sharing AI-generated campaign videos that depict him as a superhero taking on street crime and Democratic politicians. He has received a tacit nod from former President Donald Trump, but in a city where fewer than 15% of voters are Republican, that endorsement may be a double-edged sword. Bass dismisses Pratt as a political dilettante. "He is an entertainer and that's what he's doing is entertaining," she said. She points to a dip in homicides and a reduction in street homelessness as evidence of progress, while acknowledging, "I haven't always got it right." Still, the slow pace of wildfire rebuilding and persistent homelessness have eroded public confidence. The primary election is Tuesday, and unless a candidate wins a majority, the top two will advance to a November runoff. Democratic strategist Garry South expects Bass and Pratt to emerge, though he questions whether Pratt's online antics will translate into votes from the city's older, more affluent electorate. For Bass, the challenge is convincing Angelenos that she deserves more time to finish the job.
why_it_matters: The LA mayor’s race shows that politics isn’t just for lifelong politicians—celebrities can use their fame to challenge incumbents. For teens, this could shape how they think about voting: should you support a candidate because they’re entertaining, or because they have a proven record on issues like homelessness and disaster response?

background_read: Los Angeles is the second-largest U.S. city, with a mayor elected every four years. Karen Bass made history in 2022 as the first Black woman to hold the office, after a long career in the state legislature and Congress.
Wildfires have become a recurring nightmare in Southern California; recent blazes have destroyed thousands of homes, often exposing tensions over city preparedness and mayor response times.

‘The Hills,’ which aired on MTV from 2006 to 2010, made Spencer Pratt a household name for his dramatic on-screen persona, but his leap into politics is unusual and reflects a growing trend of celebrity candidates.

California uses a ‘top-two’ primary system: all candidates appear on one ballot regardless of party, and the two with the most votes advance to a November runoff, even if they belong to the same party.
In a city where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans more than 4 to 1, any Republican candidate faces long odds, making a tacit nod from Donald Trump a double-edged sword.

perspectives.description: Pratt’s candidacy shakes up a complacent political system; his personal loss gives him an authentic voice on wildfire recovery. His social media skills could engage younger voters who usually stay home, bringing fresh energy to local democracy.

Pratt lacks any governing experience, and his campaign risks trivializing serious urban crises. Some voters view him as a stunt, and his reliance on AI-generated content and Trump’s nod could backfire in a city where Republicans are a tiny minority.

California’s top-two primary system often produces a Democrat vs. Democrat runoff in deep-blue LA, but a Republican advancing is rare. This race highlights how incumbents become vulnerable when disaster recovery drags on, even if crime statistics show improvement.

If Pratt makes the runoff, it could signal that non-politicians with fame and a grievance can seriously challenge established leaders, potentially inspiring similar outsider bids across the country. A Bass victory would reinforce the value of steady, experienced governance during crises.
